newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu says bombs must stop for peace to move.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says bombs must stop for peace to move.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday Israel would not resume peacemaking as long as Palestinian bombs kept exploding.
He spoke hours after a petrol bomb was thrown at an Israeli bus in the West Bank causing it to overturn and injuring 11 soldiers. It was the third bombing Israel blamed on Palestinians in two days.

"The peace process can't be conducted while buses or cafes are exploding or while children are in danger of a terrorist blowing them up," Netanyahu told reporters as unrest in the West Bank, touched off by Israeli settlement construction, entered a third week.
Foreign Minister David Levy vowed Israel would not order its bulldozers to stop work on a new Jewish neighbourhood in Arab East Jerusalem.
Palestinians complain the settlement pre-empts the results of final peace talks yet to come on the status of East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 and claimed by both sides.
Arabs want the settlement to top the agenda when Netanyahu meets President Bill Clinton next week for peace-saving talks but the Israeli leader said halting the violence was the first priority.
"We will discuss the urgent need for the Palestinian Authority to start battling terrorism because without it we won't be able to move forward in the process and it will get stuck quickly," he said.
Clinton, involved in Israeli-PLO deals since the first was signed at the White House in 1993, pledged to get involved again on Tuesday when he met Jordan's King Hussein in Washington.
"I'm prepared personally to do anything I can to get this process back on track and move it forward," Clinton said.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called Palestinian President Yasser Arafat twice on Wednesday to hear his views ahead of Netanyahu's visit, the Palestinian official news agency Wafa said.
Wafa quoted Arafat as telling Albright: "The Israeli settlement policy ... places the entire peace process in real danger." He said later only a halt in settlement building would calm the situation.

Asked if he would face U.S. pressure over his settlement policy, Netanyahu said: "We are not operating in such a climate. I think there's a deep understanding between Israel and the U.S. today and we both see eye to eye."
Levy said that it was the PLO, not Israel, that was coming under U.S. pressure.

"I know of appeals from the United States at the most senior levels of the administration to Arafat, among others, that the war on terror is his basic obligation," Levy told reporters after meeting foreign ambassadors in Jerusalem.
"It is our right to build in Jerusalem. Period."
Palestinian stone-throwers on Wednesday clashed north of Jersualem with soldiers who responded with teargas and rubber bullets.
In the PLO-ruled Gaza Strip on Tuesday, two Palestinians were killed in explosions that Israel said were botched suicide bombings by the Islamic Jihad group aimed at Jewish school children.

Jihad sources said the Palestinian Authority had arrested 30 of their activists in overnight raids. But the group disavowed the two bombings, charging that Israel had staged them to divert attention from its settlement policy.

"The Islamic Jihad movement in Palestine denies any responsibility for the two suspected explosions yesterday and has no link at all to them," Islamic Jihad leader in Gaza Sheikh Abdallah al-Shami said.
